articles.title: How many jobs is your state losing to AI? This dashboard tracks the cuts – and the cost
articles.author: Radhika Rajkumar
articles.content:
ZDNET’s key takeaways
- AI-related job losses impact local community economics.
- The CAIS tracker puts these losses in dollars and cents.
- Understanding how AI will change the economy still involves guesswork.
Fears of how AI will impact the economy and job availability are running rampant after a few years of steady layoffs at major companies. Much of that fear can be attributed to labs and CEOs juicing their own relevance, but some job cuts have been explicitly tied to AI’s rapid acceleration.
The Center for AI Safety (CAIS) maintains a tracker that keeps tabs on how these changes are impacting family wages.
Also: Why replacing staff with AI backfires
More from ZDNET
The Wage Loss Dashboard includes a map of where layoffs have occurred since January 2026 (it was just updated this month to include September data) and a drop-down that shows data for the entire country or an individual state. As of now, the dashboard finds just over 117,000 job cuts attributed to AI nationally this year — $8.5 billion in estimated annual wage losses.
The Wage Loss Dashboard multiplies the number of AI-attributed job cuts by the average annual salary to estimate annual wage loss. According to the dashboard, wage estimates “begin to show what those cuts can mean for households and local economies.”
The dashboard also displays the estimated average wage loss per person based on that layoff data, presented relative to everyday expenses, like a tank of gas. For the country as a whole, it’s $25 per person per year. Not much, but the numbers shift by state: In California, for example, it’s $56. That’s thanks to a much higher concentration of job cuts (just over 27,000 layoffs attributed to AI). Alaska, on the other hand, claims only 138 job losses ($14 per person).
Those aren’t the exact numbers of people laid off for AI in California and Alaska this year, however. As CAIS explains, “The dashboard estimates AI-attributed cuts for each state, converts them to estimated annual wage loss, then divides by state population to estimate the average loss per person. State estimates are not observed AI layoffs. We apply each month’s national share of cuts citing AI to that state’s announced job cuts.”
From layoffs to dollars and cents
The dashboard uses a few sources of data: monthly reporting from Challenger, Gray, and Christmas, which compiles layoff announcements from across the US by state as well as national job cuts credited to AI, and data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics on every state’s annual mean wage. CAIS also refers to population estimates from the US Census Bureau.
Also: 3 ways AI can help you ace your next job interview
In 2025, the Challenger, Gray, and Christmas reports identified over 54,000 job cuts that companies publicly linked to AI. That translates to one in 20 layoffs from last year. But tracking job losses alone is a more abstract metric than what those layoffs mean in monetary terms to the people experiencing them.
“There has been significant news coverage of job loss from AI, but it can be hard to quantify how these cuts affect the average person’s finances,” CAIS wrote of the project. “This dashboard aims to help illuminate the monetary costs of AI on American families and communities.”
As CAIS points out, the impact of layoffs shows up in ripples across grocery stores, small businesses, rent, and other local costs.
“One person’s layoff means less income for every business they support. Multiply that effect across thousands of workers in multiple industries, and you start to see the real economic weight of AI displacement,” the researchers behind the project wrote. “In addition, AI-attributed job cuts aren’t spread evenly. States with large tech and media sectors are experiencing greater impact.”
A few caveats: CAIS noted that this dashboard doesn’t include “jobs created by AI, productivity gains, re-employment, or secondary economic effects.” That’s partly because experts don’t have a consensus on whether or how much AI will stimulate the economy or outpace job displacement. AI-attributed layoffs are themselves murky: The data here are job cuts companies themselves said were tied to AI. Without a single definition for what that means or complete transparency from companies, it’s not always 100% provable that a layoff was the direct result of obsolescence or replacement spurred by AI.
Also: Companies embracing AI the most are hiring more people
“We don’t require an executive to say ‘we replaced a team with AI.’ This is a moderate standard, deliberately: it captures the broad pattern of AI-justified workforce reductions while excluding clearly unrelated cuts,” the Alliance for Secure AI wrote of its methodology.
Other trackers like Jobloss.ai, which is run by the Alliance for Secure AI, also catalog job loss data by company, date, and how explicitly companies cited AI around those layoffs. Because of how amorphous these data can be to track, Jobloss.ai only logs layoffs that meet certain criteria: at least 100 jobs in one fell swoop, accompanied by some mention of AI (or proxy terms, like “automation” and “productivity”).
The dashboard aims to make the data we do have more accessible — not to shame any particular industry or company for its AI adoption choices.
“AI is a technology being adopted by companies for many reasons,” CAIS wrote. “Our goal is to make the costs of that adoption visible, so workers, communities, and policymakers can respond with real information instead of guesses.”
Automating remote labor
The Wage Loss Dashboard also includes a section on how well AI is completing remote freelance tasks. Using data from the Remote Labor Index (RLI) benchmark CAIS co-developed, which tests agents on real-world freelance tasks like web development and video production, CAIS shows how quickly agents are evolving.
“When RLI launched, the best AI agent completed just 2.5% of projects at professional quality. Eight months later, that number has risen to 15.8%,” researchers wrote. As of now, AI can fully automate almost 16% of remote tasks, a percentage that’s doubling every 3.7 months. Claude Fable 5 comes in on top, followed by OpenAI’s GPT-5.5.
But that doesn’t mean AI is gobbling up those projects from human freelancers. RLI measures what AI models are capable of doing, not what they’re actively taking on. That said, CAIS maintains alarm about what it sees as a trend: the convergence of AI-attributed job cuts with increasingly work-capable agents.
While legislation can’t explicitly prevent companies from opting for AI systems over hiring humans in certain cases, recent laws in a few states, including the tech-sector-heavy state of California, aim to make sure firing and other disciplinary decisions aren’t completely automated by AI systems.
articles.summary:
The Center for AI Safety’s new Wage Loss Dashboard estimates that AI-driven layoffs have caused $8.5 billion in annual wage losses across the United States throughout 2026.

### Key Points
- The dashboard tracks over 117,000 job cuts explicitly attributed to AI by companies since January 2026.
- California faces the highest economic impact, with an estimated $56 in annual wage loss per person due to a high concentration of tech-sector layoffs.
- Data is compiled using reports from Challenger, Gray, and Christmas, Bureau of Labor Statistics wage data, and US Census Bureau population estimates.
- The Remote Labor Index shows AI agents can now complete 15.8% of professional freelance tasks, a figure that is doubling every 3.7 months.
- The tracker excludes potential economic benefits like job creation or productivity gains, focusing solely on the monetary impact of workforce displacement.

### Why it Matters
Quantifying the financial impact of AI-related layoffs helps policymakers and communities move beyond speculation to understand the tangible economic consequences of automation. By visualizing these losses, the dashboard highlights how AI adoption creates uneven regional impacts that ripple through local businesses and household stability.

articles.title: Russian man linked to deadly London hospitals hack arrested
articles.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
articles.content:
- Published
German police have detained a Russian man accused of being part of a cyber-crime gang which caused chaos at London hospitals and contributed to a patient's death.
The hack of blood testing company Synnovis in 2024 led to disrupted pathology services across several London hospitals and was the first cyber attack in history to be directly linked to a death.
The BBC can confirm German detectives are now including the incident in their investigation into the detained Russian and his associates.
Separately, the BBC has learned that British police are examining whether its own inquiry may lead to an unlawful killing case - potentially a world first in cyber-crime.
The detained suspect is a 28-year-old Russian man named by German press as Vladimir K.
He was arrested in Japan in May when he travelled to the country for a holiday.
According to German officials, the suspect's holiday plans were intercepted and he was arrested by Japanese police when he entered the country.
He is accused of being one of the core members of the Qilin cyber-crime gang - which has allegedly hacked more than 4,000 organisations since 2024 and extorted more than $140m (£105m) from victims.
Vladimir K was wanted in Germany for hacking into a logistics company in September 2024, encrypting data on its systems and extorting it for around $160,000 in cryptocurrency.
While his extradition was first reported in early October, external, the BBC can now confirm German police are including the Synnovis hack in their investigations.
Synnovis hack
Synnovis is diagnostics and pathology service which operates as a partnership between the hospitals and German company Synlab.
A critical incident was declared at some London hospitals after the provider was targeted by Qilin on 3 June 2024, with blood transfusion services severely disrupted, operations cancelled and emergency patients diverted elsewhere.
King's College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, one of two trusts heavily impacted, confirmed a year after the hack that one patient had also "died unexpectedly".
A spokesperson for the trust said a number of contributing factors led to the patient's death including "a long wait for a blood test result".
"The patient safety incident investigation identified a number of contributing factors that led to the patient's death," they said at the time.
A similar attack in 2020 by a different hacker group on a hospital in Düsseldorf in Germany led to a negligent homicide investigation being opened after an elderly patient died.
It was later dropped after medical experts concluded the patient's condition was so severe that they would have died regardless of the issues caused by the cyber-attack.
Prosecutors could also not definitively prove that it was the direct cause of death.
In total, the Synnovis hack in 2024 disrupted more than 10,000 appointments and caused weeks of disruption.
The hackers also threatened to publish the data on their dark net website unless Synnovis paid a ransom.
The criminals eventually published the highly private data online after no ransom was paid.
At the time, they told the BBC the hack was not just for the money but to protest the UK's lack of help in the Russian war on Ukraine.
But the hackers did not say if they were from Russia or Ukraine, and their claims were dismissed as an attempt to distance themselves from the cyber-crime extortion tactics Qilin were known for.
The group, which has been tracked since 2022, is behind a string of criminal hacks targeting schools, hospitals, companies, councils and health organisations.
It was also behind the high profile and disruptive hack on Japanese beer maker Asahi in October 2025.
It is very rare for hackers to be arrested in Russia as its government refuses to co-operate with Western law enforcement requests.
articles.summary:
German authorities are investigating a detained Russian national, identified as Vladimir K., for his alleged role in a Qilin cyber-crime gang attack on London’s Synnovis pathology services.

### Key Points
- German police are investigating Vladimir K., a 28-year-old Russian national arrested in Japan, for his alleged leadership role in the Qilin cyber-crime syndicate.
- The June 2024 ransomware attack on Synnovis disrupted blood testing services, leading to thousands of cancelled appointments and the death of one patient at King's College Hospital.
- Qilin has targeted over 4,000 organizations since 2022, extorting more than $140 million and recently attacking companies like the Japanese beer manufacturer Asahi.
- British police are currently evaluating whether the Synnovis incident could result in an unprecedented unlawful killing prosecution related to a cyber-attack.
- The hackers published sensitive patient data online after Synnovis refused to pay a ransom following the disruption of critical hospital pathology operations.

### Why it Matters
This case represents a potential legal milestone as authorities consider whether cyber-criminals can be held criminally liable for patient deaths resulting from infrastructure attacks. It highlights the escalating threat posed by ransomware groups to critical healthcare systems and the complex challenges of international cooperation in prosecuting cyber-crime.

articles.title: What Is Happening With India’s Unified Payments Interface (UPI), the World’s Largest Real-Time Payments System?
articles.author: Nick Corbishley
articles.content:
For the first time since its launch a decade ago, merchants will soon have to pay fees to use the system. Some are suggesting that Washington may be behind the move.
In September, India’s Narendra Modi government unveiled a radical change to its Unified Payments Interface (UPI), the country’s instant digital payment system. That change involved the introduction of fees for the first time since its pilot launch in 2016. In September, the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) said a 0.4% fee would apply from October 15 (i.e. yesterday) to certain UPI payments above 2,000 rupees ($21) made to businesses by customers.
The initial announcement sparked fears that the fees could raise expenses for businesses, and by extension their customers, and discourage them from using the system. As those fears rose, the authorities made a partial U-turn. On October 13, just two days before the fee was to come into effect, the NCPI postponed the rollout until after the Diwali festival. But it is only a temporary respite.
UPI is the world’s largest real time payments system, with over 500 million users. In August alone, it processed 24.51 billion transactions worth ₹29.82 trillion ($314 billion). However, one of the main reasons for UPI’s undeniable success is that it is (or at least was) free to use for everyone. Many vendors originally made the switch to UPI because it was promoted as a free, convenient payment solution.
Launched in 2016 as a private-public partnership, UPI lets people send and receive money instantly through mobile apps, much like Brazil’s Pix system. The speed and ease of use has made it an integral part of the Indian economy, used by everyone — from small vendors to large corporations. As Business Times notes (with the media’s usual disdain for cash), “paying for goods no longer involves handling grubby old currency notes.”
The payment rails undergirding the system are operated by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), an umbrella organisation established as a not-for-profit initiative by major banks. The underlying protocol standardises real-time bank-to-bank transfers so that any bank or wallet can talk to any other without closed, proprietary walls.
This has allowed private companies to build consumer and merchant apps that sit on top of the public payment rails. Until now, the government, banks and payment companies have borne the cost of running and expanding the system, which is currently dominated by two foreign-owned apps: Walmart’s PhonePe and Alphabet’s GooglePay, which together enjoy around 80% market share by value of UPI transactions.
The new charge, known as the Merchant Discount Rate (MDR), is expected to help cover some of those costs, and will be distributed among payment system providers — including banks — to support operations and continued expansion, the finance ministry press release stated. That’s the official reason, but it may not be the only one. As some are pointing out, the US government may also have played a part in the decision.
Interesting Timing
The announcement of the introduction of the MDR came just as India and the US are working to finalise their bilateral trade deal. This has fuelled speculation that the Modi government was pressured by the Trump administration into imposing the fee. Earlier this week, Congress Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh said the government had broken the trust of UPI users and asked whether it had done so on behalf of US companies to appease Trump.
While there is no definitive proof to back that assertion, Washington has persistently pushed most of its trade partners to create a level playing field in their respective digital transaction ecosystem, reports India Express:
Since UPI’s launch in 2016, US payments market intermediaries Visa and Mastercard have cited loss of potential business as consumers in India increasingly turned to free UPI payments rather than using cards.
The Delhi-based think tank Global Trade Initiative (GTRI) said that the companies object to the “Zero transaction charges for UPI and RuPay, government promotion of RuPay, and RuPay’s early access to credit-card payments through UPI. This has strengthened RuPay and reduced the fee income of US card companies, it said.
It said that the two companies operate under a model where banks, payment processors and card networks earn fees from merchant transactions. A widely available, interoperable and zero-Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) platform, such as UPI, limits this revenue pool. An MDR is levied on merchants by banks that process payments to help meet transaction processing, settlement and infrastructure costs.
Further, RuPay challenges their position by providing an Indian card network that can be integrated closely with domestic policy objectives, GTRI said.
In March, the United States Trade Representative (USTR) had classified India’s digital payment policies “favouring” domestic players as a foreign trade barrier. Such barriers in various sectors are prominent demands under the proposed US-India trade deal.
The USTR said that “it has expressed concerns related to the inability of US electronic payment services suppliers to participate in the UPI ecosystem, including credit transactions on UPI on a level playing field with RuPay”.
“In November 2020, National Payment Corporation of India (NPCI) announced a market share limitation of 30% (measured by transactions) for third-party app providers initiating online payments made through India’s UPI. While this market share cap for third-party payment apps was originally mandated for January 2023, the NPCI has deferred enforcement, with the current deadline set for December 2026. As of December 31, 2025, two US-owned EPA suppliers together processed more than 80% of all UPI transactions,” USTR said. These suppliers are Walmart-backed PhonePe and Google Pay.
In other words, the USTR is concerned not only about the risk of UPI and its accompanying global card payment network, Rupay, eroding the market share of VISA and Mastercard in India (and potentially beyond), but also about India’s plans to reduce the dominance of the two US-owned payment apps, Walmart’s PhonePe and Alphabet’s GooglePay, over the UPI space.
Parallels With Brazil
This is not the first time the US has tried to bully a country into changing its indigenous payment system. As we have previously reported, Brazil’s development of Pix, a publicly owned and controlled digital payments system that has reduced the country’s dependence not only on Visa and Mastercard’s global duopoly but also on the mobile payment apps of US tech giants, has caused consternation on Wall Street and Silicon Valley, and by extension Washington DC.
The Office of the US Trade Representative began investigating PIX last year, warning that Brazil has given an unfair advantage to the digital payments system by requiring all banks to offer it. According to the NY Times, US trade authorities are also concerned that, by protecting consumer data that Pix collects, the Brazilian government is hurting American companies that use such information to make business decisions and develop new products.
“U.S. companies see this data as critical,” said Ignacio Carballo, a senior consultant at Payments and Commerce Markets Intelligence, a research firm based in San Francisco. “This places a lot of power in the hands of Brazil’s government.”
By embracing a largely publicly led digital payments infrastructure that cuts out the usual middle men, Brazil has turned financial innovation on its head. In most advanced economies, cash’s dominant role in the retail payments system has been eroded by digital payment alternatives, mainly from the private sector, in particular contactless debit and credit cards. Mobile wallets operated by US tech giants are also on the rise.
This has been a massive boon for Visa and Mastercard, which have done everything they can to supplant their biggest rival (to date), cash. In Brazil, however, Pix has not just overtaken cash; it has overtaken everything. As an article in Rest of World notes, it overtook debit card transactions in January 2022 and credit cards in February 2022, and now dwarfs transactions via credit cards, debit cards, bank slips, wire transfers, prepaid cards, and checks combined.
One major difference between Pix and UPI is that Pix is a public payments system created, owned, and operated by the Central Bank of Brazil (BCB) whereas UPI is a private-public system that is already dominated by two US-owned apps. Also, Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has resisted US pressure to bring Pix into line. A few months ago, he rejected any possibility of Pix being altered or privatised in order to benefit US financial interests.
“We defend Pix from any attempt at privatization. Pix is from Brazil. It’s public, it’s free and it’s going to stay that way.”
That said, Lula may soon no longer be president of Brazil, if recent polls for the second round of the upcoming presidential elections are any indication. Lula already lost the first round to his main rival, Flavio Bolsonaro, who has already agreed to make certain concessions on Pix. As the tweet below explains, Bolsonaro is benefitting from the support not only of the US and Israeli governments but also US tech firms like Meta.
A Sticky Dilemma
Back in India, the proposed imposition of a fee on UPI leaves Indian business owners facing a sticky dilemma: absorb the additional expense themselves or pass it on to their customers. As a direct result, these transaction charges are likely to raise the prices of basic goods and services. Everything from food items and fuel to routine retail purchases over 2,000 rupees will effectively become more expensive for ordinary shoppers.
Unless, of course, they go back to cash, which continues to play a vital role in the Indian economy, even as digital payments have exploded. Indeed, the amount of cash in circulation continues to grow as its share of everyday payments shrinks, reports the BBC:
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) – the country’s central bank – now has 176 billion banknotes in circulation. It’s printing 28-30 billion fresh ones across six denominations annually and retiring roughly 21 billion. It is a vast logistics operation.
And yet, as Unified Payments Interface (UPI) digital transactions surge towards a billion a day, cash sloshing around the economy keeps climbing at a brisk pace.
The puzzle is not that Indians still use cash – 94% of transactions were cash-based as recently as 2019, according to new research by Anirudh Tagat, Mehmet Ozmen and Pushpa Trivedi. It is that cash is growing even as its share of everyday payments shrinks.
“The cash paradox has been examined globally, and India is a unique and novel case study of the same given the scale of both cash and non-cash payments,” Tagat, an economist who studies Indian payment behaviour, told the BBC.
He notes that the phenomenon of cash growing alongside digital payments has been especially prominent since the 2007-08 global financial crisis, with Bank for International Settlements research showing a similar pattern worldwide.
In Tagat’s framing, currency still serves three purposes – as a means of payment, a store of value and a hedge against calamity. Apps are replacing only the first. That helps explain why digital payments alone cannot tell the whole story of cash demand.
It will be interesting to see what consequences the introduction of fees to UPI has for India’s native payment system. After all, the Modi has done more than any government in Indian history — and more than most governments around the world — to promote digital payment methods.
It was the Modi government, with the support and guidance of the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, that launched India’s demonetisation campaign in 2016, whose disastrous consequences Jerri Lynn Scofield covered in great deal for this site. It was the Modi government that launched UPI just months earlier, as well as Aadhaar, India’s biometric digital identity system, years earlier.
There have been suggestions that USAID, the CIA’s soft-power arm, played a key role in promoting UPI. It is certainly coincidental that months after the launch of UPI, USAID announced the launch of a new initiative, called Catalyst of all things, in partnership with the Indian finance ministry, to scale digital payments systems in India.
A Brief Delay in Implementation
On Tuesday, the National Payment Corporation of India announced that it had decided to postpone the rollout of fees on UPI until after the Diwali festival. From Reuters:
“Diwali, which will be celebrated across India on November 8, typically marks the peak of consumer spending in Asia’s third-largest economy, with shoppers splurging on cars, clothes and home appliances”:
The proposed fee, which would end more than six years of zero-cost UPI payments in India, had drawn opposition from retailers…
The delay in implementation would likely allow payments firms to upgrade systems and not pass on costs to customers, while addressing issues that retailers may face during the festive period, Reuters reported last week, citing sources…
Shares of digital payments firms Paytm (PAYT.NS), opens new tab, Pine Labs (PINL.NS), opens new tab and One MobiKwik Systems (ONEM.NS), opens new tab gained 1%, 1.8% and 1.3%, respectively, after the news.
“The notice…brings certainty that the MDR (Merchant Discount Rate) is going to be implemented and there is no more scope of any pushback…versus the earlier uncertainty around the timeline,” said Rahul Jain, director of research at Dolat Capital.
“That is a positive for the companies,” he added.
Said companies presumably include VISA and Mastercard.
articles.summary:
India’s National Payments Corporation has postponed the introduction of a 0.4% merchant fee on Unified Payments Interface transactions, sparking debate over potential US influence on domestic policy.

### Key Points
- The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) planned a 0.4% fee on UPI transactions exceeding 2,000 rupees starting October 15.
- The rollout is now delayed until after the Diwali festival to avoid disrupting peak consumer spending.
- UPI, launched in 2016, currently processes over 24 billion monthly transactions and has remained free for users and merchants since inception.
- US trade representatives have previously criticized India’s digital payment policies for allegedly favoring domestic players over firms like Visa and Mastercard.
- Walmart’s PhonePe and Alphabet’s Google Pay currently control approximately 80% of the UPI market share by transaction value.

### Why it Matters
The introduction of fees threatens to increase costs for Indian businesses and consumers, potentially slowing the rapid adoption of digital payments. This policy shift reflects broader geopolitical tensions as the US government pushes for a level playing field for American financial firms within India’s massive digital economy.

articles.title: Tech stocks tumble as AI debt fears rattle Wall Street
articles.author: Mary  Cunningham
articles.content:
Financial markets slumped on Friday as investors bailed on technology stocks amid concerns that companies exposed to artificial intelligence are starting to wobble.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite tumbled 573 points, or 2.1%, to end at 26,140, closing out its worst week since June. The broader S&P 500 and blue-chip Dow Industrial Average sank 1.1% and 0.3%, respectively.
Chipmakers and other tech companies have been under pressure this week as investors worry about the heavy borrowing associated with the emergence of AI and the rapid buildout of thousands of data centers required to provide computing power for AI models.
So-called neocloud companies like CoreWeave, which provide the brute computing power AI models need to function, were particularly hard hit. That's because they are financing much of their capital expenditures through debt and equity issuance rather than cash flow, raising investor concerns about mounting debt, market analyst Adam Crisafulli, head of Vital Knowledge, told CBS News.
Shares of CoreWeave slid nearly 12% on Friday and dropped roughly 24% this week as investors nervously eye its mounting debt. Micron Technology fell 5.6%, Advanced Micro Devices dropped 6%, Broadcom was down 4.5% and Intel lost 5.8%.
Elsewhere on Wall Street, Tesla shares fell 2.1% after the electric vehicle company unveiled a new that appears capable of thrusting itself into the air.
The downturn on Friday came amid concern about whether the AI company Anthropic, soon set to go public, will be able to maintain its revenue momentum, Crisafulli said in a note to investors. Anthropic investors are now considering valuing the company at $1.5 trillion, down from the original target of $2 trillion, Reuters reported on Thursday.
Inflation moving in wrong direction
Also rattling investors this week were fresh signs that and moving further away from the Federal Reserve's 2% annual target.
Yields on the 10-year U.S. Treasury bonds — a key benchmark for mortgages, credit cards and other loans — held steady at 5.1% on Friday. Earlier this month, to their highest level in more than two decades amid concerns over inflation and rising U.S. government debt.
The hot inflation readings this week could spur the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates at its next meeting on Oct. 28-29, according to some economists. For now, most Wall Street traders expect the central bank to keep its short-term rate unchanged, but the odds of a rate hike at the Fed's December meeting have jumped to 74.3% from 50.2% a month ago, according to CME FedWatch, which tracks Fed funds futures prices.
On Friday, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh offered no hints about potential interest rate policy moves while attending a meeting of financial leaders in Bangkok. The Fed at its last meeting in September, bringing the federal funds rate to between 3.75% and 4% — its highest level since December 2025.
articles.summary:
Technology stocks led a broad market decline on Friday as investors grew concerned over the high debt levels of AI-focused companies and persistent inflationary pressures impacting interest rates.

### Key Points
- The Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.1% to 16,140, marking its worst weekly performance since June.
- CoreWeave shares fell 12% on Friday, contributing to a 24% weekly decline amid investor scrutiny of its debt-financed capital expenditures.
- Major chipmakers including Micron Technology, Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom, and Intel saw share prices fall between 4.5% and 6%.
- Reports indicate Anthropic may lower its valuation target to $1.5 trillion ahead of its upcoming public offering.
- CME FedWatch data shows the probability of a Federal Reserve interest rate hike in December has risen to 74.3% due to stubborn inflation.

### Why it Matters
The market downturn highlights growing investor skepticism regarding the long-term profitability of the capital-intensive artificial intelligence sector. If inflation remains elevated, the Federal Reserve may be forced to maintain or increase interest rates, which would further tighten borrowing conditions for technology firms and broader financial markets.

articles.title: 'Something was thrown out with the bathwater when we moved to modern smartphones': Clicks co-founder Jeff Gadway on bringing physical keyboards back to mobile phones
articles.author: christinep2424@gmail.com (Christine Persaud) , Christine Persaud
articles.content:
I fondly remember owning my first BlackBerry, and then my second ... and third. The smartphone was a sign of prestige, a device you could fit in your pocket with both a screen (later also a touchscreen in some models) and a miniature QWERTY keyboard. It was genius. That is, until elongated, touchscreen-only phones started coming to market, namely the first iPhone. Suddenly, BlackBerrys weren't so trendy anymore.
What's old becomes new again, however — a statement that fits almost every industry, from fashion to music and even tech. Clicks Technology, a U.K.-based hardware company with team members who previously worked for BlackBerry and within the BlackBerry space, is leaning into this trend. Growing from its first keyboard case, there are two devices coming this year: the Clicks Power Keyboard, which is now shipping, and the hotly anticipated Clicks Communicator, which should launch in December.
"Something was thrown out with the bathwater when we moved to modern smartphones," Jeff Gadway, co-founder of the company (and former marketing director at BlackBerry), explained in a recent interview. His company aims to bring it back — and possibly a little magic to a market that could sorely use some fresh ideas.
I saw both devices in prototype form at CES 2026 earlier this year, and in an interview with Gadway, discussed how the company is bringing razzle dazzle back to mobile.
Clicks then and now
Clicks introduced its first keyboard case for iPhone in 2024, eventually expanding to make cases for select Android phones, too. To say people were excited would be an understatement. "It was like catching lightning in a bottle that first year," Gadway told me during a recent podcast interview.
Interestingly, it wasn't just nostalgia-fueled business executives but also younger folks from the digital native generations who were intrigued. Young adults who had never used anything but a touch- or voice-controlled phone loved the concept as much as they are now learning to love vinyl, CDs, and wired earbuds.
The company has since developed the Power Keyboard, a MagSafe enabled keyboard accessory you can use with any MagSafe-enabled phone or case, or any Bluetooth input device, for that matter. The Communicator is an Android phone reminiscent of a BlackBerry Bold that combines a small screen with a miniature QWERTY keyboard.
Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android
The Power Keyboard is universal
The Power Keyboard solves the biggest issue with the original Clicks Keyboard Case: needing a fitted case for every model phone. Instead, this version is magnetic, clipping vertically or horizontally onto the back of any MagSafe-enabled phone or phone case and functioning as a power bank with a slide-out keyboard.
It isn't limited to phones: Use it handheld with a tablet or even as a Bluetooth mini keyboard for your smart TV. If you've ever attempted to enter a password into an app using your TV's remote and on the on-screen keyboard, you know how frustrating that experience can be. Gadway says the use cases run the gamut, from students using this in class with their phone instead of bringing a laptop, to CEOs, writers, and musicians being productive on the go.
Clicks Communicator reminds you what a phone is for
Taking things a step further, the Clicks Communicator is designed to remind us of the true purpose of a mobile phone: communication. Newer smartphones are designed for content consumption and creation with bigger screens, cameras, processors, and batteries, says Gadway. "What if you could build a phone that was really optimized for communication?"
There are two ways you might use the Communicator. The first is as a secondary phone with its own plan or tethered to your primary device. Maybe you have a company-provided phone on which you aren't permitted to download personal apps. The Communicator can be that secondary device to keep in touch with family, access banking and social media apps, play games, and more. The difference between the Communicator and another smartphone is that the smaller, utility-type screen makes this possible, but it's not optimized for going down the rabbit hole of endless scrolling.
The second is as a primary phone, which Gadway told me is how a lot of pre-order customers have said they want to use it. The Communicator sits between a dumbphone, which eliminates access to distracting apps altogether, paring down the experience to bare bones communication, and a full-featured premium smartphone.
The Communicator is a full Android 17 device, though, with access to the Google Play Store, a MediaTek Dimensity 8300 processor, a 50MP main camera, and a 24MP front-facing camera. Clicks even upgraded the RAM to 12GB prior to the official launch. It has legacy features you won't find in most modern phones, like a 3.5mm headphone jack and microSD card slot to expand the built-in 256GB storage.
The key is in the design: a touchscreen occupying the top three-quarters (4.03 inches, 120Hz) and a bottom keyboard. It's a constant reminder that this isn't a phone to doomscroll TikTok and Instagram or get caught up in mobile games. You can do that. But you won't want to, and that's a good thing.
Other simple features are meant to further encourage focus, like a signal light, similar to the HiLight button in the Google Pixel 11 Pro series phones. Customize it with illuminating colors so you know when an incoming call or message is from your mom, child, spouse, or business partner versus a spam call or an old friend you don't have time to chat with right now.
Clicks is working with Niagara to build a custom Android launcher that can curate messages from your favorite apps on the home screen. Triage these apps, Gadway explains, to help prevent you from getting "sucked into side quests."
"What we're doing with Niagara," he explains, "is creating a version of this that taps into the hardware of Communicator using the touch-sensitive keyboard to scroll through your messages, and the keys themselves to delete, reply, forward, or mark as unread right from that home screen without ever having to actually go into the app itself. So, it's a much more purposeful home screen experience."
Clicks represents a return to form
Modern smartphones do more than ever. But there's something inherently missing from the experience. It stems from nostalgia, for those who grew up using phones with keyboards. But there's also value from a usability perspective for a younger generation who never put their hands on one.
Gadway says that with the original Keyboard Case, 40-45 percent of buyers had never used a BlackBerry before. "They wanted to reshape their relationship with technology, have some tech that was a little more intentional, a little more purposeful, and that allowed them to get their screen real estate back and have a more satisfying tactile experience."
"Touchscreen smartphones are amazing," Gadway said recently. "They do so many things. And yet they lack some of that tactility and the ability to accomplish certain things from your phone that you wait to do back at your desk."
Originally, Clicks was positioned, at least in the minds of those who clamored to get a look at the original case years ago, as a throwback to simpler times. Today, with the latest generation products, it's evident that a physical keyboard is no longer just catering to the BlackBerry faithful. "There is a much bigger audience than we expected," says Gadway. Touchscreens and voice activation aren't going anywhere. But there's something about tactile feel that even the younger generations yearn to experience, too.
Christine Persaud has been writing about tech since long before the smartphone was even a "thing." When she isn't writing, she's working on her latest fitness program, binging a new TV series, tinkering with tech gadgets she's reviewing, or spending time with family and friends. A self-professed TV nerd, lover of red wine, and passionate home cook, she's immersed in tech in every facet of her life. Follow her at @christineTechCA.

articles.summary:
Hardware company Clicks Technology is reviving the tactile smartphone experience with its new Power Keyboard accessory and the upcoming Android-powered Clicks Communicator device featuring a physical keyboard.

### Key Points
- The Clicks Power Keyboard is a magnetic, MagSafe-enabled accessory that functions as both a physical keyboard and a power bank for various mobile devices.
- The Clicks Communicator, launching in December, is an Android 17 smartphone featuring a 4.03-inch 120Hz display and a dedicated physical QWERTY keyboard.
- The Communicator includes a MediaTek Dimensity 8300 processor, 12GB of RAM, 256GB of storage, a 3.5mm headphone jack, and a microSD card slot.
- Clicks is partnering with Niagara to develop a custom launcher that allows users to manage messages directly from the home screen using the physical keyboard.
- The company reports that nearly half of its original keyboard case customers had never used a BlackBerry, indicating broad interest in tactile, intentional technology.

### Why it Matters
These devices cater to a growing consumer desire for more intentional, less distracting mobile experiences that prioritize communication over endless content consumption. By blending modern Android capabilities with nostalgic hardware, Clicks is carving out a niche for users seeking to reclaim screen real estate and improve productivity through tactile input.

articles.title: Why education IT teams must protect both human and machine identities
articles.author: Anne Cutler
articles.content:
At the start of every school year, schools, colleges and universities across the UK race to onboard thousands of new students, faculty and staff members, provisioning accounts, issuing credentials and connecting a wave of new devices to institutional networks.
That operational pressure creates opportunities for attackers, and this year, AI is amplifying the threat more than ever. Not only are phishing campaigns more convincing, but a hidden layer of unmanaged machine identities is expanding the cyber attack surface.
VP of Global Communications at Keeper Security.
Attackers are persistent and the education sector remains a top target with many facing cyber attacks weekly. The UK Government’s cyber security breaches survey revealed that 27% of further and higher education institutions reported experiencing a breach or attack at least weekly, compared to 14% of primary schools and 20% of secondary schools.
Navigating the expanded threat window
The education sector is one of the highest targeted industries for ransomware, credential theft and data breaches. For hackers, schools and universities present an appealing combination of high-value data, including student records, financial information and research, alongside underfunded IT departments and an enormous, ever-rotating user base.
The back-to-school season intensifies this pressure. Bulk account creation, mass device enrolment and a surge of third-party application onboarding all happen simultaneously, creating a greater risk of misconfiguration and excessive access rights. The UK Government found that no tier of the education sector had a majority of institutions compliant with all of the government’s Cyber Security 10 Steps.
Just 14% of primary schools, 23% of secondary schools, 33% of further education colleges and 45% of higher education institutions had covered all 10. As thousands of new identities and devices enter this already insecure environment, gaps in security controls can become harder to identify and manage.
AI has made cybersecurity threats significantly more dangerous. The same government survey found phishing to be the main threat identified by institutions that had suffered a breach, and those emails can now precisely mimic communications from student funding offices, IT helpdesks or university leadership, with none of the traditional red flags that once made them easy to spot.

Keeper Security’s research into AI and cybersecurity in education found that 41% of schools have experienced AI-related cyber incidents, including phishing and misinformation, while 90% of education leaders expressed concern about AI-related cybersecurity threats. Yet only one in four respondents felt very confident recognizing AI-enabled threats such as deepfakes or AI-driven phishing.
As AI makes social engineering attacks more convincing, education institutions need to reinforce human awareness with stronger identity and access controls that do not rely on users spotting every malicious message.
The hidden attack surface: non-human identities in EdTech
As students and staff begin the new academic year, IT teams will rightly be focused on securing human accounts, but there is another, much larger population of digital identities that can easily escape attention: Non-Human Identities (NHIs).
NHIs are now embedded throughout modern education environments, from service accounts that synchronize student records with learning platforms to API keys connecting third-party applications, digital textbooks and payment systems.
Machine identities and certificates authenticate everything from campus Wi-Fi and smart boards to lab equipment and security cameras, while cloud workloads automate backups, research pipelines and administrative processes. Similarly, AI agents powering admissions chatbots, helpdesks and grading tools are adding yet another layer of identities and access privileges that institutions need to manage.
These identities are essential to keeping schools and universities running, but they can also create significant security gaps when credentials are rarely rotated, old integration tokens remain active or automated accounts are granted more access than they need.
Unlike employees and students, NHIs are not naturally caught by onboarding and offboarding processes. Without a complete inventory, organizations can struggle to know which identities exist, who owns them and what they can access.
The cybersecurity conversation in education has historically centered on protecting students, teachers and administrators, but the machine identities powering modern EdTech deserve the same scrutiny, because regardless of whether a breach stems from a human or machine, the impact is the same.
Back-to-school is a useful opportunity to review the full identity estate – both human and non-human – remove identities that are no longer required and tighten access for those that remain.
How education IT teams can reduce their risk
For most institutions, the fundamentals of managing humans are manageable. The critical gap is visibility and governance over the NHIs that power modern EdTech, like service accounts, API tokens, machine certificates and AI agents that multiply with every new integration. Security teams should take these steps to help secure NHIs and humans alike.
Enable multi-factor authentication
As the new semester begins, organizations should ensure MFA is enforced across all faculty, staff and student accounts, with new users defaulted into it from the moment they are provisioned. MFA remains a fundamental defense against credential-based attacks.
Audit privileged access
Many accounts give users privileged access beyond what’s necessary for their role. Privileges should be audited for both humans and non-humans. This includes removing access for departed employees and students, retiring expired service accounts and eliminating unnecessary administrative privileges.
Deploy enterprise password managers
Password security remains one of the hardest problems for security teams to solve. Awareness and training can provide students, faculty and staff with the knowledge on how to create strong passwords, but converting that knowledge into practice is difficult because password reuse, written passwords and browser storage remain common. Enterprise password managers remove that gap, enabling users to create and store strong, unique credentials.
Build a non-human identity inventory
You can’t secure what you can’t see. Schools should catalogue every service account, API key, machine certificate, cloud identity and AI agent. Establish ownership and record what each identity can access.
Establish credential rotation policies
It’s important to establish credential rotation policies for machine identities, paying particular attention to AI agents and third-party EdTech integrations added for the new school year. The Canvas learning management system hack, reported in April 2026, affected almost 9,000 educational institutions globally – a reminder that third-party credentials require the same rotation discipline as internal accounts.
Third-party access should be regularly examined and security teams should scrutinize the security of all current and potential partners and suppliers.
Updated training
Security awareness training needs to keep pace with the threat landscape, particularly around phishing, where AI-generated messages may be indistinguishable from legitimate institutional communications. Staff should independently verify unusual requests rather than relying on visual cues alone
Getting ahead of the rush
Back-to-school will always put education IT teams under pressure, but it does not have to create an open window for attackers. As institutions begin the new academic year, security must extend beyond onboarding students and staff to understanding every identity with access to critical systems and data.
By enforcing strong authentication, tightening privileged access, improving credential hygiene and gaining visibility over the growing population of non-human identities, IT teams can significantly reduce their exposure.
Security should be treated as a continuous discipline, not a back-to-school checklist. It is critical that every human and machine identity has the right access, for the right purpose and for only as long as it is needed.

articles.title: I've spent over $3,000 on ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini, and only one was worth the money
articles.author: Mahnoor Faisal
articles.content:
Something I remember particularly well about the early days of generative AI is how quickly people developed an aversion to the idea of paying for yet another subscription. I could understand why! We were already paying monthly for everything from streaming services to cloud storage, and suddenly, using a chatbot just to draft a quick email or (unfortunately) write an essay was going to cost another $20 a month.
In fact, when ChatGPT Plus first launched in February 2023, Reddit was filled with people questioning whether a chatbot could possibly be worth that much. Fast forward a few years, and I've somehow managed to spend over $3,000 on subscriptions to ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini alone.
After spending that much money, I've come to realize that paying for an AI subscription isn't necessarily a waste of money. Paying for the wrong one, however, absolutely can be! So, here's the only one I'd happily continue paying for...
ChatGPT Plus is the easiest subscription to justify
OpenAI has finally won me over
If you'd told me six months ago that I'd be recommending a $20 ChatGPT Plus subscription over a $100 Claude Max subscription, I'd have looked you right in the eyes and laughed. However, over the last few weeks, ChatGPT has undeniably jumped to the very top of my list, and it's not even a particularly close competition anymore.
For starters, OpenAI's models have gotten significantly better. I've noticed the difference most when using Codex and Claude Code side by side, especially when giving both tools the exact same task. There was a time when Claude Code would consistently deliver better results, particularly when it came to building polished interfaces and figuring out what I wanted without needing me to spell out every little detail. Lately, though, the tables have turned. Codex has been doing a much better job of understanding my intentions, making sensible decisions on its own, and delivering finished products that actually feel finished.
Even when I preferred Claude for coding, I was always vocal about how ChatGPT still excelled as a general-purpose AI assistant. Whether I needed help researching a topic, understanding a complicated concept, brainstorming ideas, or simply figuring something out, ChatGPT was almost always the first tool I'd turn to. Now that Codex has caught up with, and in some cases surpassed, Claude Code in my own testing, I'm finding fewer and fewer reasons to pay for a separate Claude subscription.
The biggest reason, though, is the limits. Claude frankly has absurd usage limits, and I manage to hit my weekly limit just three days into the week! On the contrary, I can get through an entire week of using Codex on my $20 ChatGPT Plus subscription without running into nearly as many restrictions. Considering I was paying five times as much for Claude Max, it's becoming increasingly difficult to justify spending that kind of money when the cheaper alternative lets me get more work done.
Claude has lost the edge it once had
Oh, how the tables have turned
While I've already addressed most of the reasons I don't prefer Claude nearly as much as I used to, I think the biggest one is that it no longer has the unique edge that once made it so easy to recommend. It's not necessarily that Claude has gotten significantly worse. Rather, competing LLMs have caught up with, and in some cases surpassed, the things Claude used to do better than everyone else. And when that happens, all the little frustrations you've been willing to overlook suddenly become a lot harder to ignore.
I also feel like Anthropic has sort of slowed down in the last few months. I've always praised the company for staying ahead of the curve and introducing features that genuinely change how people use AI, rather than simply chasing whatever its competitors are doing. Lately, though, it feels like OpenAI has been moving at a much faster pace, rolling out new features and improvements that give me more reasons to keep coming back. That's not to say Claude has stopped improving, but for the first time in a long while, I find myself getting more excited about what OpenAI is doing than what Anthropic has up its sleeve.
Unfortunately, it's not just the pace of innovation that's been bothering me. A couple of months ago, I wrote an entire article about how exhausting Claude had become to use, particularly for research. Despite using its most capable model at the highest effort setting, I kept finding that Claude would rush through research tasks, overlook useful sources, or answer questions without even bothering to search the web.
In one experiment, I gave Claude and ChatGPT the exact same research question. Claude spent roughly a minute and a half putting together its answer, while ChatGPT spent around 12 minutes digging into the topic. The difference in the quality and depth of their responses was enough to make me question what I was paying so much more for.
Then there's the fact that Claude has occasionally taken it upon itself to decide how I should use my remaining allowance. I've had Claude Code discourage me from continuing a task because I was approaching my usage limit, even though I was perfectly happy to use whatever I had left. I understand warning users before they run out, but I don't think a tool I'm paying $100 a month for should be making that decision for me.
None of this means Claude is a bad AI assistant. Far from it! There are still things I prefer about Claude, and I wouldn't hesitate to recommend trying it. But recommending Claude and recommending a paid Claude subscription are two very different things. With the competition getting better and the frustrations piling up, I just don't see enough reasons to keep paying for Claude Max anymore.
Gemini is the weakest reason to pay for Google AI Pro
Everything but the chatbot makes it worthwhile
Google AI Pro is a slightly different story. Unlike ChatGPT Plus and Claude Pro, where the main selling point is access to better AI models and higher usage limits, Google's subscription comes bundled with a bunch of other perks that make it surprisingly easy to justify.
For instance, I use NotebookLM practically every day for studying, and I genuinely wouldn't hesitate to pay $20 a month for its premium features alone. The higher limits are incredibly useful, especially when I'm working with multiple lectures, readings, and presentations. So, the fact that Google AI Pro includes an upgraded NotebookLM experience alongside 5TB of cloud storage, Gemini integrations across Google's productivity apps, and access to other tools like Flow and Antigravity makes it a pretty compelling package.
There's even YouTube Premium Lite included in select countries, which is a nice bonus if you're someone who spends a ridiculous amount of time watching YouTube. And if you already rely heavily on Gmail, Google Docs, and Drive, I can absolutely see Google AI Pro being the subscription that makes the most financial sense for you.
The problem, at least for me, is Gemini itself. While Google's models have certainly improved, I still find myself turning to ChatGPT or Claude for most of the things I'd normally use a general-purpose AI assistant for. Whether it's brainstorming ideas, researching something, or tackling a complicated task, Gemini rarely ends up being my first choice.
In every comparison where I've pitted Codex, Claude Code, and Antigravity against each other, Antigravity has, without fail, been the one that disappointed me the most. It's not necessarily that it can't get the job done, but the results often feel far less polished than what its competitors deliver. I've had instances where Antigravity declared a project finished despite leaving out features I'd explicitly requested, and others where I had to step in to fix problems that ideally should've been caught during testing.
That's ultimately why I find Google AI Pro a little difficult to recommend purely for Gemini. The subscription itself offers tremendous value, particularly if you're already invested in Google's ecosystem, but I don't think the chatbot or coding experience alone is compelling enough to make me choose it over ChatGPT Plus.
So, all that to say, the subscription I can most easily recommend right now is ChatGPT Plus. Claude would be my next pick if you're looking for an AI assistant primarily for writing or coding, though I'd think twice before splurging on its more expensive tiers. I'd only recommend Google AI Pro if the AI itself isn't your main reason for subscribing, and you're more interested in perks like NotebookLM, cloud storage, and integrations with Google's other services.
articles.summary:
OpenAI’s ChatGPT Plus has emerged as the most justifiable AI subscription, outperforming competitors like Anthropic’s Claude and Google’s Gemini in coding capabilities, research depth, and overall usage value.

### Key Points
- ChatGPT Plus is currently favored for its superior coding performance via Codex and more generous usage limits compared to Claude.
- Anthropic’s Claude Max subscription is criticized for high costs, restrictive usage caps, and inconsistent research quality compared to OpenAI’s models.
- Google AI Pro provides value through bundled perks like 5TB of cloud storage and NotebookLM, despite Gemini’s performance trailing behind competitors.
- The author reports spending over $3,000 on AI subscriptions, concluding that ChatGPT Plus offers the best balance of utility and price.
- Competitive pressure has forced rapid innovation, with OpenAI currently outpacing Anthropic in feature rollouts and model reliability.

### Why it Matters
Choosing the right AI subscription is increasingly important as monthly costs for these tools accumulate for professional and personal users. Evaluating these services based on actual performance and usage limits helps consumers avoid paying for redundant or underperforming software in a rapidly evolving market.

articles.title: Waymo Puts Toronto on the Map for Its Robotaxis
articles.author: Dashia Milden
articles.content:
Waymo is bringing its autonomous ride services across the border to Canada for the first time.
The company said in a blog post on Friday that its robotaxis will be available for you to book rides in the app in the Toronto area in 2028. It will start with a limited number of its mainstay Jaguar I-Pace electric SUVs, and will add more over time.
But if you’re in Toronto, you can expect to see Waymo cars, driven by humans, in the coming days as the company maps local street networks and acclimates its autonomous technology to traffic patterns and driving conditions.
Waymo will test in select Toronto neighborhoods, including Liberty Village, St. Lawrence Market and Yorkdale. It has also built a sixth-generation Waymo Driver autonomous driving system to navigate diverse environments, including the extreme winter weather Toronto faces in the colder months. A Waymo representative did not immediately respond to a request for further comment.
The company is also partnering with Toronto-based Element Fleet Management for vehicle maintenance, validation driving and customer service.
Waymo launched its fully autonomous ride service featuring electric vehicles in 2018. The ride service is currently available in the US in places including Miami, Phoenix and the San Francisco Bay Area. Earlier this year, Denver, San Diego, Las Vegas and Tampa were added to the list of available cities.
Sign-ups to ride with Waymo in Toronto and track the progress of the Canadian launch are now open on Waymo’s website.
articles.summary:
Waymo plans to launch its autonomous ride-hailing service in Toronto by 2028, marking the company's first international expansion beyond its current operations in several major United States cities.

### Key Points
- Waymo will deploy a fleet of Jaguar I-Pace electric SUVs to provide autonomous transportation services throughout the Toronto area.
- Human-driven vehicles will begin mapping local streets and testing traffic patterns in neighborhoods like Liberty Village and Yorkdale immediately.
- The company developed a sixth-generation autonomous driving system specifically engineered to navigate Toronto’s diverse urban environment and extreme winter weather conditions.
- Toronto-based Element Fleet Management will provide essential support services, including vehicle maintenance, validation driving, and customer assistance.
- Interested users can currently sign up on the official Waymo website to receive updates and track the progress of the Canadian launch.

### Why it Matters
This expansion represents a significant milestone for Waymo as it tests its autonomous technology in a new international market with challenging seasonal weather. Successfully navigating Toronto’s climate could provide the company with critical data to scale its robotaxi operations into other cold-weather regions globally.

articles.title: Fed chair warns AI spending could fuel inflation and pledges to contain prices
articles.author: MAX ZAHN
articles.content:
Fed Chair Kevin Warsh warns of AI 'shock' for economy, pledges to contain inflation
Warsh said AI would ultimately generate wealth but the path may be "very bumpy."
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh warned of a potential "shock" to the U.S. economy delivered by a rise in artificial intelligence spending, pledging to contain price increases as a flood of private sector funds drives up demand.
"If you’re a central banker, you’re in the business of trying to ensure stable prices and full employment, you’ve got to recognize this as a shock," Warsh said in Bangkok, Thailand, at a conference organized by the International Monetary Fund.
A surge in AI spending has helped boost the U.S. economy in recent quarters. In theory, an onrush of investment in activities like chip manufacturing and data center construction could put upward pressure in general on consumer prices, unless the demand is offset by a new supply of goods and services.
"It’s obviously hitting the demand side of the economy before it’s hitting the supply side of the economy," Warsh said.
Warsh, who took the helm of the Fed in May, has previously weighed in on the potential impact of AI on the labor market and wider economy.
On Friday, Warsh reiterated his optimism about AI, saying the technology would ultimately generate added productivity and wealth.
But, Warsh added, "the path from where we are to there is likely to be a very bumpy one."
"We really don’t know what the market structure will be of these new technologies," Warsh said. "Who's going to be making the money?"
Warsh acknowledged other shocks faced by the U.S. economy, including "shocks of war and military conflict."
The outbreak of the Iran war in February imposed a historic oil supply shock and caused an acceleration of price increases in many countries. A U.S. government report issued this week showed inflation had climbed to a 4-month high in September as the Middle East conflict continued to drive up gasoline prices.
Prices rose 3.7% in September, according to new data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Inflation stands more than a percentage point higher than the Fed's target rate of 2%.
"It’s hard to be in a discussion with central bankers and not compare notes and hear the same thing about the surge in prices," Warsh said on Friday.
He later added: "I’ve heard resolve from my colleagues around the world to deliver price stability. I’ve certainly delivered that resolve."
Price hikes prompted the Fed to raise interest rates a quarter of a percentage point in September, marking the central bank's first rate increase since 2023.
An increase to the benchmark interest rate aims to slash inflation by slowing the economy and eating away at demand, though the policy typically yields results after a lag time lasting several months.
The next meeting of Fed policymakers takes place on Oct. 28, just days before the midterm elections.
Consistent with his approach in previous public appearances, Warsh opted against issuing a forecast about what the central bank may do at its meeting later this month.
"I don’t pre-judge meetings. I don’t believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings we have over the balance of this year," Warsh said.
Many investors appeared to interpret Warsh's posture as a sign the Fed may hold interest rates steady later this month.
As of Friday morning, investors peg the chance of the Fed maintaining current interest rates at about 86%, which marks an uptick from about 55% on Wednesday, according to CME Group’s FedWatch Tool, a measure of market sentiment.
articles.summary:
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh warned that rapid artificial intelligence investment could trigger economic shocks, pledging to prioritize price stability amid rising inflation and global geopolitical instability.

### Key Points
- Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh identified AI spending as a potential economic shock that increases demand before boosting supply-side productivity.
- U.S. inflation reached a four-month high of 3.7% in September, exceeding the Federal Reserve's 2% target rate.
- The Federal Reserve implemented a quarter-percentage-point interest rate hike in September to combat rising consumer prices.
- Ongoing Middle East conflict and the Iran war have contributed to global oil supply shocks and increased gasoline prices.
- CME Group’s FedWatch Tool indicates an 86% market probability that the Federal Reserve will maintain current interest rates at the October 28 meeting.

### Why it Matters
The Federal Reserve faces a delicate balancing act as it attempts to curb inflation without stifling the economic growth driven by emerging artificial intelligence technologies. Investors are closely monitoring these policy signals to gauge whether the central bank will prioritize aggressive rate hikes or maintain stability in the coming months.

articles.title: Reolink Home Hub 2 On-Device AI, 16MP Camera Support, and Subscription-Free Security Storage
articles.author: Jude Chukwuemeka
articles.content:
Reolink has launched the Home Hub 2, a next-generation security hub designed to make managing home surveillance footage easier through on-device artificial intelligence, expandable local storage, and centralized camera controls.
Unveiled at IFA 2026, the Home Hub 2 brings Reolink’s ReoNeura AI technology to its home security ecosystem. The device introduces Local AI Video Search, allowing users to find relevant moments in recorded footage using simple keywords instead of manually reviewing hours of video.
The hub also supports a 2.5-inch hard disk drive (HDD) or solid-state drive (SSD), along with a microSD card, giving users additional local storage options without requiring a cloud subscription. It can manage up to eight compatible Reolink cameras from a central location.
Local AI Video Search Makes Security Footage Easier to Find
One of the Home Hub 2’s main features is Local AI Video Search, powered by Reolink’s ReoNeura on-device AI engine.
The feature allows users to search locally stored recordings across connected cameras using keywords. Rather than scrolling through long playback timelines, users can search for relevant footage and go directly to the moments they want to review.
Because the searches run locally on the hub, the feature does not require a cloud subscription. This approach also keeps the search process within the user’s local security setup.
For homeowners reviewing activity around entrances, driveways, gardens, or other monitored areas, the ability to locate specific events more quickly could make everyday security monitoring more convenient.
Cross-Camera Tracking and Upcoming AI Features
The Home Hub 2 is designed to do more than search individual recordings. Its Cross-Camera Tracking feature follows a detected object across multiple cameras and combines the relevant footage into a single video.
This can help users follow activity as it moves between monitored areas, providing a more connected view of an event than reviewing each camera separately.
Reolink also plans to introduce additional AI capabilities through an upcoming firmware update.
These include:
- Custom AI Detection: Designed to let users define the types of scenarios they want the system to recognize.
- AI self-learning: Intended to help the system learn user-defined situations and provide more relevant alerts.
For example, a user could configure the system to recognize a side gate left open. These features are intended to make security notifications more relevant to individual properties, although Reolink says they will arrive in a future firmware update rather than being available at launch.
Expandable Local Storage With Encryption
The Home Hub 2 offers multiple storage options for users who want to keep security recordings locally.
Its storage configuration includes a new SATA slot that supports a 2.5-inch HDD or SSD, as well as a microSD card slot supporting cards of up to 1TB.
This combination gives users flexibility to expand recording capacity according to their needs. It also reduces reliance on cloud-based storage services, which may involve recurring fees.
Reolink says the hub uses encryption to help protect recordings against unauthorized access, including in situations where a camera or microSD card is stolen.
For households that prefer to manage their own surveillance footage, the combination of expandable storage and local AI processing is a central part of the Home Hub 2’s design.
One Hub Can Manage Up to Eight Cameras
The Home Hub 2 supports up to eight compatible Reolink cameras, including battery-powered Wi-Fi, plug-in Wi-Fi, and Power over Ethernet (PoE) models.
It supports cameras with resolutions of up to 16 megapixels and uses 2.4GHz and 5GHz Wi-Fi 6 connectivity.
The hub also creates its own local network. According to Reolink, compatible cameras can continue recording to the hub if the home’s internet connection goes down, helping preserve local surveillance coverage during an internet outage.
Users can manage connected cameras through the Reolink app, where they can view high-definition live feeds and recorded playback across multiple devices.
The app also includes a Regular Security Summary, which presents daily, weekly, or monthly statistics about motion-detection events. This gives users a way to review activity trends and jump directly to relevant recordings.
Camera compatibility and supported features may vary by model, so users should check Reolink’s compatibility information before connecting existing equipment.
App Controls, Time-Lapse Playback, and Custom Alerts
Reolink says the Home Hub 2 can be configured through the Reolink app in three steps. Once set up, users can manage their cameras and review footage from a central interface.
The app’s time-lapse feature can condense longer events into shorter videos. This can be useful for reviewing gradual changes, such as a sunrise or an ongoing construction project, without watching the entire recording.
The hub also features a built-in alarm center that can sound a siren when a connected camera is triggered. Users can choose from available ringtones or select a custom sound.
For additional notification flexibility, the Home Hub 2 supports sending alerts, including images, to Discord, Telegram, and Slack.
The product announcement notes that these integrations are supported, although availability and configuration may depend on the connected services and the user’s setup.
Works With Alexa and Google Assistant
The Home Hub 2 also supports Amazon Alexa and Google Assistant, enabling hands-free viewing on compatible displays, including Amazon Echo Show and Google Nest Hub devices.
This integration gives users another way to check camera feeds without opening the Reolink app each time.
Combined with centralized camera management and local recording, the smart assistant support helps the Home Hub 2 fit into a broader connected-home setup.
No Subscription or Monthly Fees
A key selling point of the Reolink Home Hub 2 is that its listed features are available without a subscription or recurring monthly fees.
Local AI video search, expandable storage, and centralized camera management are designed to operate as part of the user’s own security system. This may appeal to homeowners who prefer to pay for their hardware and storage rather than maintain an ongoing cloud-storage subscription.
The hub’s local network and storage capabilities also offer an alternative for users who want their cameras to continue recording locally during an internet outage.
However, users should distinguish between local recording and remote access: viewing or managing a system from outside the home may still depend on network availability and the relevant configuration.
Pricing and Availability
The Reolink Home Hub 2 is available now in the United States for $199.99.
Buyers can find more information and purchase the device through the official Reolink website.
With support for up to eight compatible cameras, expandable HDD or SSD storage, microSD cards up to 1TB, and on-device AI search, the Home Hub 2 is designed to serve as a centralized management and recording solution for Reolink camera systems.

This device offers a subscription-free alternative for homeowners who prioritize data privacy and local control over cloud-based surveillance services.
